Jewish Diaspora. The Jewish Diaspora refers to the dispersion of Jewish people from their ancestral homeland of Israel into communities across the Mediterranean, Middle East, Europe, and eventually worldwide. Beginning with the Babylonian Exile in the sixth century BCE and accelerating after Roman conquests and expulsions, the diaspora became a defining feature of Judaism, creating distinct regional communities with diverse traditions, languages, and cultural expressions while maintaining religious and ethnic identity.

The Babylonian Exile from five hundred ninety-seven to five hundred thirty-nine BCE saw King Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon conquer the Kingdom of Judah and exile its elite. Though many returned after Persian conquest, Jewish communities remained throughout the Near East. Roman subjugation and destruction of the Second Temple in seventy CE during the Jewish-Roman Wars accelerated diaspora. Romans expelled Jews from Jerusalem and suppressed rebellions, scattering communities throughout the Roman Empire.

Medieval Europe saw Jewish communities flourish in some regions like Spain under Islamic rule, Italy, and the Rhineland, but face persecution, forced conversions, and expulsions. England expelled Jews in twelve ninety. France did so multiple times. Spain expelled them in fourteen ninety-two.

Ashkenazi Jews, descendants of those in Central and Eastern Europe, developed Yiddish and distinct cultural practices. Sephardic Jews from the Mediterranean and Middle East retained Ladino and other traditions. Mizrahi Jews remained in Arab lands. Diaspora communities maintained religious practice, Torah study, and ethnic identity across centuries of dispersion and persecution, creating Judaism as a religion of diaspora, not tied to a single place.

Pogroms in Eastern Europe, especially Russia, and anti-Semitic policies drove mass Jewish migration to North America from the eighteen-eighties to nineteen-twenties, creating large communities in New York, Boston, and other cities. The Holocaust from nineteen forty-one to nineteen forty-five murdered six million Jews and devastated European Jewish communities. The Israeli state's founding in nineteen forty-eight offered a homeland and redefined diaspora identity for many Jews, creating a new chapter in the ancient history of Jewish dispersion and return.
